USMLE-style practice · Orthopedics

Acute compartment syndrome: 2

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A patient has a tense painful forearm after injury, but the radial pulse remains palpable. A trainee argues that this excludes compartment syndrome. Which statement correctly interprets the pulse finding in this clinical situation?

  1. Acute compartment syndrome
  2. Compartment-pressure assessment when needed
  3. Urgent surgical decompression
  4. Ischemic muscle contracture
  5. Preserved pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Preserved pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome

Major arterial flow can remain present while microvascular tissue perfusion is compromised.

Understanding the options

Preserved pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome
Major arterial flow can remain present while microvascular tissue perfusion is compromised.
Acute compartment syndrome
Escalating pain, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment after injury are concerning for pressure-related ischemia. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Compartment-pressure assessment when needed
Pressure measurement can support diagnosis when the examination is unreliable; it must not delay obvious emergency treatment. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Urgent surgical decompression
Established acute compartment syndrome requires urgent specialist treatment, usually fasciotomy. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Ischemic muscle contracture
Untreated ischemia can cause muscle necrosis, fibrosis and permanent contracture. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
